newsitem.title: USA: GM averts one strike continues talks on others.
newsitem.headline: GM averts one strike continues talks on others.

text.p: General Motors Corp. early Saturday averted one parts plant strike and said it would continue to negotiate past midnight deadlines to avoid two other walkouts that could severely disrupt its North American car and truck production.

The automaker said it reached a tentative agreement late Friday for a new local labor contract at a foundry in Saginaw, Mich. About 900 members of United Auto Workers Local 445 had threatened to strike the plant at 11:59 p.m. EDT Friday, a move that would have cut off supplies of pistons, piston rods and transmission parts for various cars and trucks.

GM and UAW bargainers continued to talk early Saturday morning past an 11:59 p.m. EDT Friday strike deadline at the automaker's Grand Rapids, Mich., metal stamping plant. The plant employs 2,346 hourly workers and produces doors, fenders, hoods and other sheetmetal parts for a variety of GM vehicles, including the automaker's all-new minivans.

Talks to avert another possible strike at a catalytic converter plant in Oak Creek, Wis., were recessed until later Saturday morning following talks Friday that continued past a midnight Thursday strike deadline.

A work stoppage at the 870-employee factory in suburban Milwaukee would begin to halt production at most of GM's 29 North American car and truck assembly plants within days and could affect other customers in Europe and Asia, GM officials say.

GM also is expected to resume talks on Saturday in an effort to end a strike more than seven weeks old at its Pontiac, Mich., pickup truck plant. Union officials reported that some progess had been made in those talks.

Until this week, talks at all four of the plants have moved slowly. Some analysts view the multiple strike threats at the parts plants as a move by the UAW to increase pressure for GM to settle the Pontiac walkout.
About 5,800 workers walked off their jobs at Pontiac on April 22 to underscore their demands for more jobs to ease an increasing workload. UAW Local 594 initially sought 600 new jobs.
GM has resisted, in part because a new-generation pickup truck due next year is expected to require about 30 percent fewer workers to build it.
